summary:
Mato Grosso stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and the 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism under constitutional and federal criminal provisions. Entry, visa and gender-marker rules operate on the same footing for trans visitors as for anyone else. The National Council of Justice's Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where arrested or imprisoned LGBTI people are housed: recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, placement is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference, LGBTI-specific spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Violence risk is the dominant finding for Mato Grosso. ANTRA's 9th annual dossier, released on 26 January 2026, records 3 killings of trans and travesti people in the state during 2025, against a national total of 80. That national figure is 34% below 2024, with at least 75 attempted homicides recorded in the same year and crimes marked by excessive violence. Brazil has led the global ranking of such killings since 2008, with 1,261 murders over 2017-2025, an average of 140 a year; 97% of victims were travestis or trans women, more than half aged 18-29, and 70% Black among racially identified cases.

Two features of that national pattern bear directly on a visitor's itinerary. First, 67.5% of killings occurred in interior cities rather than capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policies are harder, which raises exposure for travel beyond Cuiabá and Campo Grande. Second, Mato Grosso's 3 cases place it 12th among Brazilian states for 2025, and the state has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017. Three cases on a small population is a statistically fragile reading, but the interior-city concentration is the more durable signal.

Two state-level measures cut the other way. A decree published in Mato Grosso's official gazette on 12 March 2021 guarantees travestis and trans people the right to use their social name, accepted by state public offices and usable on badges, cards and identification documents, with state employees able to register it in internal records and official publications barred from using the civil name without consent. And on 16 April 2026 a jury sentenced businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, to 13 years and 6 months for the feminicide of the trans woman Mayla, found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside MT-485 in Sorriso, together with procedural fraud and corpse concealment; the jury held the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
The national picture behind Mato Grosso's count is uneven rather than uniformly improving. Ceará and Minas Gerais recorded 8 killings each in 2025, Bahia and Pernambuco 7 each, and Goiás, Maranhão and Pará 5 each, against Alagoas and Mato Grosso at 2 and 3 respectively; the 34% national decline therefore sits alongside continued high counts in several states.

Political participation carries its own risk. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Protection machinery has widened in ways a visitor may see reflected in local services. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, and the Sorriso jury's use of feminicide in a trans victim's case is consistent with that direction. Courts have also applied anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Practice still departs from the detention framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in Rio de Janeiro state, documenting housing in masculine-operated units and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. That study concerns Rio de Janeiro state, not Mato Grosso, and no equivalent census of Mato Grosso's prisons appears in the inventory.
localsOnly:
The social-name decree of 12 March 2021 is a state-government measure addressed to Mato Grosso residents as much as to visitors: travestis and trans people may register the social name in internal state records and systems, use it on badges, cards and identification documents, and official publications may not use the civil name without consent.

Residents bear the weight of the state's longer record. Mato Grosso has counted 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017, and ranked 12th among Brazilian states in 2025 with 3 killings.

The Sorriso conviction establishes that a Mato Grosso jury will treat the gender-motivated killing of a trans woman as feminicide, convicting Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira of 13 years and 6 months on 16 April 2026 for the January 2024 killing of Mayla, along with procedural fraud and corpse concealment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific state ordinance or protection measure beyond the 2021 social-name decree appears in the inventory for Mato Grosso; whether the state has any further instrument is unresolved on the sources provided.

The inventory contains no reporting on how Mato Grosso police, prisons or courts apply National Council of Justice Resolution 348/366 in practice, and no census of trans detainees in the state equivalent to the 2021 Rio de Janeiro study. Placement practice here is therefore not sourced.

The 3 killings recorded for Mato Grosso in 2025 are drawn from a single source, ANTRA's dossier as reported by SBT News and the Diário de Cuiabá; no independent corroboration of the individual cases, their locations or their dates is available in the inventory.

Whether the interior-city concentration documented nationally (67.5% of killings) holds specifically within Mato Grosso is not stated in the sources; the state-level breakdown by city is unresolved.
